item.description: Healing Art Show 2026 OPEN OCTOBER 2, 2026 - OCTOBER 30 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM The Healing Art Show Bloomington is a community art exhibit celebrating the connection between creativity, mental health, and well-being. item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Thu Oct 15 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Thu Oct 15 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Thu Oct 15 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Home Away from Home: Student Life on Campus — Thu Oct 15, 9:00 AM — HERMAN B WELLS LIBRARY
item.description:
Spanning across four decades—1970s to the 2000s—items including scrapbooks, photographs, student papers, and handbooks demonstrate life on and off campus. From decorating dorm rooms to chasing campus ghosts, students have always found ways to build community and make new memories. This exhibit highlights the student experience and the multitude of ways students found a sense of home, identity and belonging at Indiana University.
Source: IU Bloomington Libraries

item.title: Meet the Author: Winnifred Sullivan — Thu Oct 15, 4:00 PM — ids@iu.edu
item.description: Making a King: The Political Theology of Joan of Arc The College Arts \+ Humanities Institute and the Center for Religion & The Human present a Meet the Author talk with Winnifred Sullivan \(emeritus, Religious Studies\) in conversation with Spencer Dew \(Ohio State University\) about Sullivan's recent book, Making a King: The Political Theology of Joan of Arc \(Columbia, 2026\). Please join us for a reception following the discussion. Winni Sullivan, who has written extensively about the contradictions and paradoxes of religious freedom law in the US, has written a new book about Joan of Arc. Growing out of her teaching at IU and elsewhere, Sullivan presents a young woman of intelligence and courage who thought the religion and politics of her time differently, offering a model, perhaps, of vernacular political theology, a politics of peace free of aristocratic absolutism and greed. item.title: Safety Cabaret (Load-In) — Sun Oct 18, 9:00 AM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description:
October 18, 9am – 5pm: Load-In Load-In will use the process of bringing a production into the theatre to explore rigging, lighting, audio, staging, carpentry, material handling, working at height, hazard recognition, and communication between departments.
Load-in also creates an opportunity for technicians to learn outside their own specialties. Participants may get a closer look at why rigging needs certain information from lighting, how audio infrastructure affects other departments, why carpentry and scenic decisions can change access or workflow, and how stage management and production management coordinate all of those moving parts. The goal is not to make every technician an expert in every discipline. It is to give people a better understanding of the departments working around them so they can anticipate conflicts, ask better questions, and communicate more effectively.

Using a real technical-rehearsal environment, participants will explore communication between performers, stage management, rigging, lighting, audio, scenic, and other production personnel.
The day creates space for questions that are often difficult to address during a normal production schedule. What information does lighting need from the performer? What does audio need before rehearsal begins? How do scenic or rigging decisions affect blocking? What does stage management need from each department? How should a performer ask about a technical element they do not understand? How should a technician explain a concern without relying on jargon? These conversations are valuable not only for performers, but also for technicians. A lighting technician benefits from understanding what the audio department is trying to accomplish. item.title: Safety Cabaret (Load-Out) — Tue Oct 20, 9:00 AM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description:
October 20, 9am – 5pm: Load-Out Load-Out will examine the production process in reverse. Participants will see how quickly a theatre changes when equipment begins coming down, scenery starts moving, cables are removed, rigging systems are operating, and areas that were safe during a performance become active work zones. Load-out also provides another opportunity for departments to better understand one another’s priorities. The sequence in which equipment comes down matters. Access needed by one department may affect the work of another. Schedule pressure and fatigue can make communication even more important. Participants will be able to see how planning, coordination, and mutual understanding can make load-out both safer and more efficient.
Participants may register for individual days or the full three-day event. Registration and additional event information: https://delong.ludus.com/show_page.php?show_id=200534364 https://delong.ludus.com/show_page.php?show_id=200534364

item.description:
Early in 1922, the Indiana University Baseball team received an invitation from Waseda University professor Iso Abe (Abe Isoo, aka "Father of Japanese baseball") to travel to Japan to play a series against both Waseda and Keio Universities. Abe believed that building these sorts of relationships would lead to a more harmonious world and had begun organizing baseball exchanges in 1905. Please stop by this pop-up event to learn more!
